title: Geometrically Constrained Stenosis Editing in Coronary Angiography via Entropic Optimal Transport
claim: Prior noise-initialized soft-guided generation yields seed-dependent, inconsistent outputs; fixing a structural start state with path-level guidance gives a deterministic path.
layout: 2 stacked rows, left-to-right, shared t=0→1 time arrow, zoom-in insets
description: Two horizontal rows compare generation trajectories along a shared time arrow running from t=0 to t=1. The top row, labeled Conditional Diffusion, shows two random-noise seeds (z1, z2) plus a gray Condition box (mask/prompt). Each seed denoises through four angiogram frames into a coronary image, and the two final vessel patterns differ. Dashed lines link a small box on each result to a magnified crop. The bottom row, OT-Bridge Editor (Ours), starts from an edited vessel-structure map S* instead of noise. A blue banner, GPG Path-level guidance, sends arrows down onto each intermediate frame. The row ends in a zoomed crop, and a red label reads Deterministic Generation Path. Red text marks the proposed method. The eye goes first to the top row's noisy seeds, then to the blue banner.
caption: Conceptual comparison between conditional diffusion and OT-Bridge Editor. OT-Bridge Editor fixes the start state S∗ (edited vessel-structure) and enforces hard, path-level guidance (GPG) within a Schr¨odinger-bridge formulation, producing a deterministic generation path toward the target.
abstract: The scarcity of high-quality imaging data for coronary angiography (CAG) stenosis limits the clinical translation of automated stenosis detection. Synthetic stenosis data provides a practical avenue to augment training sets, improving data quality, diversity, and distributional coverage, and enhancing detection precision and generalization. However, diffusion-based editing commonly relies on soft guidance in a noise-initialized reverse process, offering limited pixel-level precision and structure preservation. We propose the OT-Bridge Editor, which reframes localized editing as a constrained entropic optimal transport (OT) problem and leverages geometric information to steer the generation path, enabling stronger geometric control. Extensive experiments show that our synthesized angiograms consistently improve downstream stenosis detection, yielding substantial relative gains of 27.8% on the public ARCADE benchmark and 23.0% on our multi-center dataset, supported by consistent qualitative results.
